summary: Describes current practices in NAS products that go beyond the scope of the earlier RADIUS RFCs, 2138 and 2139. It records what vendors actually do. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Companies added extra tricks to their dial-in boxes that the official rules did not cover. This writes down those tricks.

questions: what are vendor extensions in radius
subtitle: A snapshot of vendor-specific RADIUS extensions and their interoperability challenges

tldr.problem: RADIUS protocol, standardized for Network Access Servers in the mid-1990s, has proven too narrow for real-world dial-in operations. Vendors have built dozens of features completely outside the protocol, creating incompatibilities and making interoperable products difficult to deploy.
tldr.mechanism: This memo documents the ad-hoc extensions vendors have implemented across attributes, data types, message codes and operational functions, showing how far practice has diverged from the RFCs.
tldr.outcome: The practices are now de-facto standards in the field, but lack standardization and vendor coordination, severely hindering interoperability. Future AAA protocols need to address these functions formally.

today: RFC 2882 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. The vendor-specific practices it documents remain in widespread use in mature NAS products, though interoperability challenges persist without formal standardization.

sections.title: The Gap Between Standards and Practice
sections.content:
When the RADIUS working group chartered the protocol in 1995, dial-in terminal servers were simple: authenticate a user, hand out an IP address, track the session. Real-world Network Access Servers (NASes) have grown far more complex. They manage tunnels, allocate resources, enforce policies and perform operations the original RFCs never imagined.

Rather than wait for formal updates, vendors have implemented these features outside the protocol, using the RADIUS structure and format but adding operations and semantics well beyond the RFC documents. These ad-hoc extensions have become de-facto standards in the field but introduce significant problems: each vendor does it differently, interoperability suffers, and administrators must reverse-engineer unknown behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: The original rule book for dial-in boxes was small and simple. Companies needed to do much more, so each invented their own additions. Now nobody can be sure what anyone else's box will do.

sections.title: Vendor Attributes and Conflicts
sections.content:
RADIUS attributes are identified by numbers. The base RFCs defined about 70 attributes, with values 192-223 reserved for experimental use and 224-240 for implementation-specific use. Attribute 26, the Vendor Specific Attribute (VSA), was added to allow vendors controlled expansion through a structured format.

In practice, attributes 92-255 are already in use by vendors, and different vendors claim the same numbers. To manage this, RADIUS servers must know the vendor type of each NAS client, so they can map attributes to the correct internal meaning. Some servers maintain a single large vendors file; others use multiple dictionaries indexed by vendor and model. This vendor-specific context becomes essential for any server to work with multiple NAS brands.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like having a postal code system where different towns use the same codes for different places. The post office has to look up who is sending the mail to deliver it to the right place.

sections.title: Data Types and Message Extensions
sections.content:
The base RADIUS protocol defines four data types: 32-bit unsigned integers, strings (1-253 bytes), IPv4 addresses and Unix timestamps. Practice has expanded this with tunnel attributes that use an optional tag byte to support multiple attribute sets, and special types like binary packet filters and phone strings that servers parse and validate.

Alongside attributes, vendors have introduced 26 new message types beyond the original 6. Examples include password change (types 7-9), resource management (types 21-26) for IP address and tunnel allocation, and session management (types 29-34) for token card passcode negotiation and menu-driven interactions. Some of these messages are used between the RADIUS server and other resource servers, making RADIUS a glue protocol for functions it was never designed to carry.
sections.plainLanguage: The original post has room for a name, address, and message. Companies added special codes on the envelope for routing mail through extra services, and new kinds of messages that the post office had to learn to handle.

sections.title: Operational Functions Beyond Authentication
sections.content:
Vendors have implemented several operational features using RADIUS extensions. Password change lets remote users request password updates (rejected by the working group for security reasons, but deployed anyway). Authentication modes add message types for token card servers to negotiate passcode changes. Menu systems use the Reply-Message attribute and Access-Challenge messages to present text menus and receive selections from dial-in terminals.

Pseudo-user requests take advantage of the RADIUS server's database capability by sending Access-Requests with well-known usernames to query information like static IP routes or the Message of the Day. This dual-purpose use of authentication messages for non-authentication queries creates security risks if not carefully guarded with proper Service-Type values.
sections.plainLanguage: Dial-in boxes learned to ask the RADIUS server for things beyond just user passwords: menu choices, special routes, configuration data. The server has to know which requests are real users and which are just database lookups.

sections.title: Resource Management and Dynamic Control
sections.content:
Many NAS implementations need to allocate and free dynamic resources at runtime. IP address allocation ranges from simple (letting the RADIUS server assign from a pool) to complex (delegating to an outboard server). Some implementations track concurrent logins using SNMP, telnet monitoring or analysis of accounting messages to enforce per-user session limits.

Authorization changes allow active modification of running sessions. Vendors have added server-to-NAS messages (e.g., Change Filters Request, Disconnect Request) to dynamically alter firewall filters or terminate sessions in response to policy changes or registration with an authorization server. This two-way communication model is largely absent from the original RADIUS design.
sections.plainLanguage: As users are logged in, the dial-in box needs to hand out IP addresses and keep track of how many sessions are open. Some companies even let the server tell the box to change filter rules or hang up on a user while they are still connected.

sections.title: Where This Stands
sections.content:
RFC 2882 is an Informational document, not a standard. It captures a snapshot of vendor practices as of July 2000, with the explicit disclaimer that practices and numeric assignments may change. The document serves as motivation for why future AAA protocols must formalize these functions rather than leave them to ad-hoc vendor extension.

The practices remain in use today in mature NAS products, but interoperability remains a challenge. Each combination of NAS vendor and RADIUS server requires custom configuration and dictionary files to map vendor-specific attributes correctly. The document illustrates why the working group eventually moved to define more comprehensive successor protocols and why explicit standardization of common functions is essential.
sections.plainLanguage: This paper writes down what companies were doing in 2000. Many of the same tricks are still used today, but nobody tried to standardize them properly, so products still do not understand each other very well.
